questions.q: Why does LTV Global rely on Snowflake rather than any single transactional system for cross-system reporting?
options: Because no single system of record owns the full picture across Salesforce, Meridian, and LedgerPoint, so none can answer a question spanning all three alone
Because Salesforce cannot generate any reports at all
Because LedgerPoint is being retired and replaced by Snowflake
Because Snowflake is the system of record for Account and Contact data
questions.explain: Each transactional system can answer its own slice of a question, but none owns the full cross-system picture — Snowflake exists specifically to assemble that picture from extracts of all three.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce feed Snowflake via Bulk API rather than a synchronous API?
options: Because Bulk API is required for any integration involving a data warehouse
Because synchronous APIs cannot authenticate using Named Credentials
Because a full or incremental extract at LTV Global's record volumes is exactly the large, asynchronous job type Bulk API is designed for
Because Snowflake only accepts data through Bulk API by technical requirement
questions.explain: Bulk API is designed for large asynchronous data volumes, which fits a nightly extract of LTV Global's record counts far better than a synchronous API meant for smaller, real-time operations.

questions.q: Why does LedgerPoint's Snowflake feed reuse the same nightly batch files from the Lesson 14 reconciliation process instead of a separate export job?
options: Because LedgerPoint cannot generate more than one file per night under any circumstances
Because maintaining two separate batch processes against a fragile legacy system would duplicate effort and risk when one export already exists
Because Snowflake requires all data to arrive through Salesforce only
Because the reconciliation process and the Snowflake feed must always use different files by Salesforce's own rules
questions.explain: Reusing the existing nightly export avoids maintaining two fragile batch processes against the same legacy mainframe system, which would be unnecessary duplicated risk for no added benefit.

questions.q: Why does the dealer parts-pricing API use External Services while the credit-check API uses a plain Apex callout?
options: There is no real reason; the choice is arbitrary and inconsistent
Because the credit-check API does not use a Named Credential at all
Because External Services cannot be used for any financial data under Salesforce policy

External Services fits a stable schema a declarative tool (Flow) calls directly for live pricing lookups, while the credit-check API's on-demand, Apex-driven usage pattern doesn't benefit from a declarative schema the same way
questions.explain: The lesson frames this explicitly as a deliberate fit-to-use-case decision: External Services suits the dealer portal's declarative, live-pricing need, while the credit-check and shipping-tracking APIs' on-demand, code-driven usage patterns are better served by plain Apex callouts.

questions.q: Why does every external API integration in this design use a Named Credential?
options: Because centralizing authentication details means a credential rotation or endpoint change is a configuration update, not a code deployment, and keeps secrets out of version control
Because Named Credentials are only required for APIs accessed by external portal users
Because Named Credentials eliminate the need for any field-level security
Because Named Credentials are a legal requirement under GDPR
questions.explain: Named Credentials centralize endpoint and authentication details so that changes don't require a code deployment, and they keep secrets out of version control — a maintainability and security benefit, not a GDPR-specific requirement.
